An existing lump sum is not a paycheque. This guide is about money already invested being drawn down. Earnings saved from each pay are invested as they arrive; they are a different question from whether to stage a lump sum, covered in the phased-investing guide.

Bigger is not always better. With a crash in year 1, a two-year reserve ends near CAD 208,057 and a three-year reserve near CAD 165,427, below having no reserve, because the part not needed during the fall stays idle.

Crash in year 1: a one-year reserve lifts the 30-year value from about CAD 192,052 to about CAD 210,900. It pays the withdrawals through the fall and early recovery, so far fewer cheap units are sold.

Crash in year 1: about CAD 192,052, roughly CAD 35,368 less. Two years in, the gap is only about CAD 9,000 (CAD 494,401 against CAD 503,423); it compounds from there because the lost units never earn the later returns.

Crash in year 29: about CAD 211,712, roughly CAD 15,708 less than no crash. The late crash still costs something, because withdrawals are taken during it, but the balance it hits is much smaller and there are few years left for the damage to compound.
Fees. The 5% return is after fees. A management expense ratio comes out of the fund every year, in good and bad years alike, so a higher fee works like a permanently higher withdrawal rate.

Limits. One crash, smooth returns in ordinary years, no taxes inside the model, no changes in spending and no other income such as CPP, OAS or a pension. Real crashes can be deeper, can come more than once and can take years to recover, or may not recover in real terms within your horizon.

No crash: the same reserve lowers the 30-year value from about CAD 227,420 to about CAD 184,789, because CAD 22,500 sat in cash at 3% for 30 years instead of in the fund at 5%.

The account changes the tax, not the market risk. CRA says amounts paid out of a RRIF are taxable on receipt, so a gross withdrawal must cover the tax as well as the spending. CRA says TFSA withdrawals are tax-free, and the amount withdrawn is added back to contribution room on January 1 of the following year. In a non-registered account each redemption can realize a capital gain or loss measured against the average cost of the units; the non-registered withdrawal guide follows that split. Selling units in a crash in any of these accounts has the same effect on the units left.

Why a balanced fund. A fund that holds both bonds and stocks usually falls less than an all-equity fund in a crash, which reduces the units sold at low prices. It can still fall a lot, and bonds and stocks have fallen together, as the 2022 example shows. The 25% fall here is an input, not a description of any fund.
A cash reserve: what it buys and what it costs

A common answer is to keep one or more years of withdrawals in cash or a short-term deposit and draw on it while the fund is below its earlier high, so no units are sold during the fall. The fourth chart tests that rule. The reserve comes out of the same CAD 500,000, earns a hypothetical 3%, and is not refilled.

Once you start living off the money, the arithmetic turns around. A fixed withdrawal of, say, CAD 1,875 a month has to be raised by selling units. When the price is low, more units must be sold for the same cash. Those units are gone before the recovery, so the fund recovers on a smaller base. This guide follows that effect through a single balanced fund, asks how much the timing of a crash matters, and tests the common remedy of keeping a year or two of withdrawals in cash.

Same returns, different order, different result

Saving from each paycheque buys more fund units when prices fall. Withdrawing a fixed amount each month does the reverse: it sells more units when prices fall, and those units are not there when the fund recovers. With the same yearly returns in a different order, a crash in the first year of withdrawals can leave noticeably less money decades later than the same crash near the end, even though without withdrawals the two would end level. A cash reserve can avoid selling during a fall, but idle cash usually earns less than the fund, so a reserve is insurance with a cost, not free protection.

So a reserve is insurance. It pays off when a fall comes early and the reserve is spent while the fund is down; it costs money in the many years when it is not used. Refilling the reserve from the fund after a recovery, or treating it as the short-term part of the portfolio’s fixed income, changes these numbers, which is why the rule here is deliberately simple. The withdrawal-source guide looks at selling whichever asset is above its target instead, and the spending guardrails guide looks at the other lever: taking a little less after a bad year.

The calculator starts with CAD 500,000 in a balanced fund at CAD 10 a unit, or 50,000 units. It withdraws 4.5% in the first year, CAD 22,500 paid as CAD 1,875 at the start of each month, and raises that by 2% a year. In ordinary years the fund earns a hypothetical 5% after fees.

The effect becomes severe when the withdrawal rate is high or the fall is deep. At a 5% first-year rate and a 40% fall, the no-crash path still has about CAD 12,580 after 30 years, while the early-crash path runs out in month 345, during year 29. At a 6% rate and a 25% fall, the early-crash path runs out in month 268 and even the no-crash path runs out in month 277, during year 24. At 4% and a 25% fall, both last comfortably and the early crash leaves about CAD 31,000 less. Change the inputs to see where your own plan sits; none of these figures is a forecast.

The increase was not steady: the September index rose 0.5% from 2019 to 2020 and 6.9% from 2021 to 2022. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range, which is why the calculator starts with a 2% yearly increase in the withdrawal. That is an assumption, not a promise; you can change it. A withdrawal that rises each year makes the order of returns matter more, because the amounts being sold keep growing.
The mirror image of saving from each paycheque

The reserve pays withdrawals only while the fund is below its earlier high, so the fund is not sold during the fall. It helps most when the crash comes early and costs something when there is no crash, because the cash earns 3% instead of the fund's 5%. It is not refilled here. A reserve changes which asset is sold when; it does not change the returns, and a fall that lasts longer than the reserve still forces fund sales.

The second chart shows units sold each month. Without a crash the first withdrawal sells 187.5 units and the twelfth about 179.3, because the price has risen. With the crash, the twelfth withdrawal needs about 244.1 units at a price near CAD 7.68, and the first withdrawal of year two, now CAD 1,912.50, needs 255. Over the first two years the crash path sells about 818 more units for exactly the same cash paid out. The price is back above CAD 10 by month 22, but the fund has fewer units to benefit from it.

When you withdraw a fixed amount each month, a market fall early on forces you to sell more fund units at low prices. See why the same returns in a different order leave different amounts, how inflation raises the withdrawal you need, and what holding a year or two in cash costs and buys.

While you are working, a fixed amount invested from each paycheque buys more units of a fund when the price is low and fewer when it is high. That is the familiar argument for dollar-cost averaging, and it is why a fall in the market while you are still contributing is less damaging than it looks: the paycheque contributions made through a crash buy cheap units.
